summary: Desoximetasone is a potent synthetic topical corticosteroid available as cream (0.05% and 0.25%) and gel (0.05%), indicated for the relief of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as psoriasis and eczema. A thin film is applied twice daily. Like other potent topical steroids, prolonged use, large surface areas, or occlusion can lead to systemic absorption with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression, and local effects such as skin atrophy, striae, and folliculitis.
indications: Relief of the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses

dosage.d: Apply a thin film of cream 0.05%, cream 0.25%, or gel 0.05% to the affected area twice daily; rub in gently
dosage.n: Use the smallest amount needed; reassess if no improvement

dosage.d: Use lowest amount for shortest duration; safety not established for chronic use
dosage.n: Children are at greater risk of HPA-axis suppression and systemic toxicity

admin: Apply a thin film only to affected skin and rub in gently
Avoid use on the face, groin, and axillae unless directed
Do not use occlusive dressings unless specifically instructed (increases absorption and local adverse effects)
Wash hands after application; avoid contact with eyes
Discontinue when control is achieved; reassess diagnosis if no response within 2 weeks
moa: Like other topical corticosteroids, desoximetasone has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties. The precise mechanism is unclear but is thought to involve induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins (lipocortins), which control the biosynthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting the release of their common precursor arachidonic acid. This reduces local inflammation, edema, and pruritus in responsive dermatoses.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to desoximetasone or any component of the preparation
relative: Application to large body surface areas or under occlusion (systemic absorption)
Use on thin skin (face, intertriginous areas) - higher risk of atrophy
Cutaneous bacterial, fungal, or viral infection at the application site
Use in young children for prolonged periods
monitor: Local signs of atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, folliculitis
Signs of HPA-axis suppression with extensive/prolonged use
Worsening or secondary infection at the treated site

preg: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women; corticosteroids are teratogenic in animals when given systemically. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the risk; use the smallest amount for the shortest time and avoid extensive areas or occlusion.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in breast milk; it is not known whether topical application results in sufficient systemic absorption to be detectable in milk. Use caution in nursing women, and do not apply to the breast/nipple before nursing.
renal: With normal cutaneous use, systemic absorption is limited and no renal dose adjustment is required. Excessive or occluded application could increase systemic exposure.
hepatic: With normal cutaneous use, systemic absorption is limited and no hepatic dose adjustment is required.

moderate: Other topical agents that increase skin absorption or irritation at the same site
minor: Systemic corticosteroids - additive risk of HPA suppression with extensive concurrent topical use
interactions.diagnostics: Extensive use may suppress the HPA axis; an ACTH stimulation test can assess recovery if suppression is suspected.

emergency: Manifestations of Cushing syndrome from systemic absorption

monitoring: Treated skin for atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, and folliculitis
Signs of HPA-axis suppression in extensive or prolonged use, especially in children
counsel: Apply a thin layer to the affected skin twice a day and rub in gently
Do not cover with airtight bandages unless your doctor tells you to
Avoid use on the face or skin folds unless directed
Do not use longer than prescribed - stop when the rash clears
Tell your doctor if the skin thins, stretch marks appear, or the condition worsens
pk: Anti-inflammatory effect within hours to days of application
Local effect; systemic peak depends on amount, area, skin integrity, and occlusion
Absorbed fraction metabolized hepatically and excreted renally
Dosed twice daily to maintain effect
Store at controlled room temperature; keep tightly closed and out of reach of children
pearls: Potent topical steroid - reserve for short-term control of responsive dermatoses
Occlusion, large surface area, and inflamed/thin skin all increase systemic absorption and HPA suppression risk
Avoid the face and skin folds where atrophy and striae develop readily
Children absorb proportionally more - limit area and duration
If no improvement in ~2 weeks, reconsider the diagnosis (e.g., undiagnosed infection)
missed: If you miss an application, apply it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not apply extra to make up.
overdose: Topical overdose is unlikely to cause acute problems, but excessive or prolonged application can be absorbed systemically and produce HPA-axis suppression and features of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) and hyperglycemia. Manage by reducing frequency or discontinuing; gradual withdrawal may be needed if suppression has occurred.
